provenance.editionCredits:
El Concierto para clarinete en La mayor, K. 622, de Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart, fue compuesto en Viena en 1791 para el clarinetista Anton Stadler, gran amigo y cofrade masón de Mozart, para clarinete y orquesta.

La orquesta que acompaña al solista consta de dos flautas, dos fagotes, dos trompas y cuerdas. Está escrito en la misma tonalidad que el Quinteto para clarinete y el Cuarteto K. 581, también destinado a Stadler.

provenance.editionCredits:
This transcription of a relatively obscure operatic selection was motivated by the performance of a vocalist for whom I hold a great deal of respect and awe.

When I was a sophomore in high school, I was in City High School's production of Mary Poppins, which received a plethora of awards and recognition from the Iowa High School Musical Theatre Awards. I played the role of Mrs. Brill, which provided me with the first of two special recognition awards from the IHSMTA that I would obtain during my high school career (the second being from my senior year, in which I played the male role of Big Jule in Guys and Dolls).

In our production of Mary Poppins, the roles of Mary and Bert were double cast, with the evening pair each receiving well-deserved leading performer awards. However, I was keenly aware of the assured vocal maturity and musicianship of the matinée Mary, who was portrayed by Evelyn "Eddy" Galstad. While I had never worked with Eddy before, I was continuously stunned by her nuanced soprano voice. Eventually, she went off to Luther College to pursue a degree in vocal performance. Her vocal gifts were ultimately met with a well-deserved financial gift — the coveted Brudos Opera Prize.

Recipients of the Brudos Opera Prize get the opportunity to perform a solo recital in recognition of their achievements. Although Eddy was originally slated to perform her recital in May around the time of her graduation, it had to be rescheduled to October due to the ongoing pandemic. Luckily, I was able to witness her performance via Luther's livestreaming service. (Here's the link to the full recital: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2OjCjN2Pyl0)

As this was the opening number to the program (and was one of several works that I had never heard of previously), I decided to transcribe it in its full form to better appreciate the stylistic details and to further appreciate Eddy’s thrilling execution of Arne's swift, high-lying vocal line.

provenance.editionCredits:
Das Lied der Deutschen, auch Deutschlandlied genannt, wurde von August Heinrich Hoffmann von Fallersleben am 26. August 1841 gedichtet. Die Melodie stammt ursprünglich aus dem 1797 entstandenen Kaiserlied von Joseph Haydn. Das Lied wurde am 5. Oktober 1841 auf dem Jungfernstieg in Hamburg erstmals öffentlich gesungen.

1922 wurde das Lied der Deutschen zur Nationalhymne bestimmt. Zur Zeit des des Nationalsozialismus wurde nur die erste Strophe gesungen. Nach 1945 war die weitere Verwendung des Liedes umstritten. Erst 1952 wurde entschieden, dass das Lied der Deutschen Nationalhymne der Bundesrepublik Deutschland blieb, wobei zu offiziellen Anlässen jedoch nur die dritte Strophe gesungen werden sollte.

Nach der Wiedervereinigung wurde im Jahr 1991 die dritte Strophe zur Nationalhymne Deutschlands erklärt.

provenance.editionCredits: The 40th symphony is one of my favorite works by Mozart. It is one of two minor-key symphonies, both of which are in g-minor, and this one is often referred to as "the great." I enjoy this one more than No. 25 because of its tragic sound, which doesn't occur often in Mozart's symphonies. No one knows for certain the intention of Mozart, but I think that this first movement shows us the inner feelings of the composer more than most of his other works, especially toward the end of his life.

Franz Schubert: Two Ecossaises
From: 18 German Dances and Ecossaises Op. 33 (D.783)
Public Domain, PianoXML typeset

The 16 German Dances and 2 Ecossaises of Op. 33 were made to be played as one single dance piece. Presumably, there should be a pause as the pianist moves from the waltz pieces to these two Ecossaises. Regardless, these pieces are fun to play as a individual pieces, as a single piece, or as the playful end of the full 18 song playlist.

provenance.editionCredits:
Based on IMSLP: https://imslp.org/wiki/Special:ReverseLookup/58214
Work Title: 6 Minuets
Composer: Beethoven, Ludwig van
Catalogue Number: WoO 10

6 minuets:
    Minuet - Trio (C major)
    Minuet - Trio (G major)
    Minuet - Trio (E♭ major)
    Minuet - Trio (B♭ major)
    Minuet - Trio (D major)
    Minuet - Trio (C major) 

Year/Date of Composition: 1796
Composer Time Period: Classical

A note on Musescore playback: There is not gap between songs but there is a weird gap in the middle. It was the best I could do and welcome suggestions on how to make it better (if it is not A LOT of work).

Playback problem explanation: The piece plays a bit strangely as the last repeat of the Trio has a 3 second pause before repeating and after the Fine the piece plays immediately into the next Minuet. The strange gaps and lack of gaps is due to the use / not use of section breaks. The section break imposes a 3 second delay which works great between pieces but in this case drives some weird playback. I tried putting the section break at the end of the Minuet section but that just makes the D.C. al Fine play the Trio over yet again which is not at all what you want.

provenance.editionCredits:
About a year after his first set of Paganini arrangements, Robert Schumann revisited the violin caprices for another six études. This time, however, Schumann was less interested in merely recreating the pieces on the piano than imbuing them with his own ideas, and as a result the Op. 10 set is generally regarded as more imaginative and less strictly pedagogical than the Op. 3. Paganini's fourth caprice was a particular favorite of Schumann's, who likened it to the second movement of Beethoven's Eroica Symphony.

Constructive criticism is greatly appreciated!

The original sheet music can be found here: https://imslp.org/wiki/6_Concert_Etudes_after_Paganini_Caprices%2C_Op.10_(Schumann%2C_Robert)

"This Caprice should be played passionately, with strong contrasts and the utmost brilliancy of colouring; not a single note in it should be without expression. While in the second Caprice, the player had to pay strict attention to precision in striking the double notes exactly together, here he may break the chromatic thirds lightly and quickly with the same fingers. In the 'Minore' the quick change from legato to staccato must be noticed; in order to execute this cleanly and well, it is advisable to begin by practising slowly. The effect of the G-minor movement will be greatly enhanced if both hands play in exactly the same gradations of tone-colour."
-Excerpt from the first publication, translated by Mevanwy Roberts in a reprint.

Constructive criticism is greatly appreciated!

The original sheet music can be found here: https://imslp.org/wiki/Etudes_after_Paganini_Caprices%2C_Op.3_(Schumann%2C_Robert)

"For the pianist, the chief difficulty of the first Caprice is that each hand is required to maintain a distinct and independent quality of tone. It is only when the different parts are all in fortissimo that both hands should play with exactly the same strength. The tempo, already rather quick, may be somewhat increased in the middle of the movement, but must return very gradually to the tempo primo towards the end, with an occasionally recurring rhythmical accentuation of the strong beats of the bar, which, if done without rigidity, produces calm both for player and hearer alike. "
-Excerpt from the first publication, translated by Mevanwy Roberts in a reprint.

Constructive criticism is greatly appreciated!

provenance.editionCredits:
"This Caprice may be regarded as an exercise in double notes for the right hand, and in leaps or skips for the left. The player need only pay attention to striking the thirds precisely together, keeping the fingers free from stiffness. This is learnt more easily and comfortably by continuous playing, than by over-practising different groups.
"In the E minor movement, the lower voice of the right hand should be very delicately joined to the last note of the arpeggio-chord, being careful to raise the thumb precisely, thus bringing out the melody in both parts more distinctly. As an exercise for the fourth finger, the third is doubled in the chords for the left hand.
"The 'Minore' (A-minor) which, as in all Paganini caprices, goes about one half slower than the 'Majore,' will not fail in its effect if it is played lightly, capriciously, and con passione."
-Excerpt from the first publication, translated by Mevanwy Roberts in a reprint.

Constructive criticism is greatly appreciated!

The original sheet music can be found here: https://imslp.org/wiki/Etudes_after_Paganini_Caprices%2C_Op.3_(Schumann%2C_Robert)

provenance.editionCredits:
About a year after his first set of Paganini arrangements, Robert Schumann revisited the violin caprices for another six études. This time, however, Schumann was less interested in merely recreating the pieces on the piano than imbuing them with his own ideas, and as a result the Op. 10 set is generally regarded as more imaginative and less strictly pedagogical than the Op. 3. The string crossings of the second caprice are condensed into one octave in order to make it playable on the piano.

Constructive criticism is greatly appreciated!

The original sheet music can be found here: https://imslp.org/wiki/6_Concert_Etudes_after_Paganini_Caprices%2C_Op.10_(Schumann%2C_Robert)

"The third Caprice stands forth more for its simple heartfelt song than as a study. The editor, very regretfully, felt obliged to omit the humorous middle movement as being altogether too unsuited to the pianoforte, thus sacrificing the character of the Caprice. He draws attention to the silent change of fingers on the same key [fingerings have been omitted], which (although less here) often produces a beautiful effect in adagio movements; also to the wide arpeggios in the left hand together with a judicious use of the pedal, which is left to the discretion of the thoughtful player. It is hardly advisable to add any more ornaments than those indicated, and least of all to make use of the turn... But even here, no limitations need be dictated to a cultivated taste."
-Excerpt from the first publication, translated by Mevanwy Roberts in a reprint.

Constructive criticism is greatly appreciated!

"In this Caprice, the editor has purposely only fingered certain notes [omitted here]. But anyone really in earnest about learning this piece, should fill up the blanks himself; for unless he has clearly made up his mind about each individual note, a complete mastery of this extremely difficult Caprice will be impossible. Although Paganini marked the time Presto, a too quick tempo would be detrimental to the grandeur of the whole. Someone else, perhaps, might have wished an interpretation from just the opposite point of view. And in any case, it would be not without interest if some more skillful hand were to undertake a second adaptation of the work.
"The peculiar difficulty in this case lies in the almost stingingly sharp emphasis to be given to certain tones, while the other voices proceed in perfect legato throughout. Here again, practising slowly is the quickest and surest way to success. In the second half the diverging parts must be individually characterized by a special touch for each."
-Excerpt from the first publication, translated by Mevanwy Roberts in a reprint.

Constructive criticism is greatly appreciated!

provenance.editionCredits:
Will H. Vodery (or Will A. Vodery. I've seen both, but probably H) is an interesting composer. On the surface it's a name I doubt anyone will know, and I myself did not know either at first. I had done no prior research on him before preparing to upload this score, and I expected to find nothing of interest, if anything at all.

How wonderfully wrong I was.

All of the following info is taken from wikipedia, so take that as you will, but it goes as follows: Vodery was an african-american composer, with speedy beginnings. Born on October 8th, 1885, to a pianist (his mother), and a teacher at Lincoln University in Philadelphia (father). From an early age his family rented rooms to theater performers, exposing him to many talented performers at the turn of the century.

From there it is mostly uneventful. In 1910 he started serving as the musical director for performances at the Howard Theater in Washing D.C, up until a year later. Over a decade later he apparently started composing for several theater shows, I.E: From Dixie to Broadway, Show Boat, etc, nothing terribly interesting (at least to me).

But the two most significant parts are these: In 1922 he apparently worked with the infamous George Gershwin for a time, providing orchestrations for Gershwin's 'Blue Monday' opera.

Secondly, Vodery was also an important influence on - not joking - Duke Ellington. This description is getting rather long so I won't go until a whole lot more detail, but I will leave this: " Also in 1929, Vodery, in his capacity as Ziegfeld's musical supervisor, recommended Ellington for Show Girl." (Also a Gershwin musical).

I encourage you to read the whole thing here, and see if more can be found: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Will_Vodery It's rare that so much can be found on such an obscure composer, but it's a very pleasant surprise to learn he did more behind the scenes than one would expect.

Please use the YouTube audio provided if possible. This piece requires human musicality—computer playing fails to do it justice.


(Unfortunately, due to a glitch that shifted my markings for when to switch to the next bar, you will need to manually scroll through the score. Sorry for any inconvenience caused by this.)


Go here to find the full score or any part as PDF files: https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1FR-yHCniukTZJeHD7EhfqQBcEOdiFK7y?usp=sharing


Out of Vivaldi's twenty-eight (according to Wikipedia, which is not entirely reputable) known double violin concerti, this one stands out for several reasons, one of which being that all movements encompass concise themes and imitation; in fact, each movement introduces a theme in the first violins, followed by exact imitation in the second violins.

Note the first movement for its development. Vivaldi would typically leave the majority of development to the ritornello and introduce great amounts of new material in the soloists' parts; however, Vivaldi gradually morphs the soloists' melodies into new, exciting shapes throughout the movement.


Another interesting aspect of the concerto is its second movement's opening. The style is in stark contrast to nearly every slow movement Vivaldi wrote, the only similar slow movement I can think of being the andante from another double violin concerto, RV 313, which is fugal.


The third movement is intense and fiery, the fastest of the three movements, which is the usual tempo scheme for a Vivaldian concerto. Out of the three movements, it is the most "normal", but this does not make it any less valuable than the preceding movements.


I decided to copy down this piece for these reasons, as well as the fact that individual parts seem not to be available on the Internet. Enjoy!

provenance.editionCredits:
Updated to Musescore 3.6
 
This movement starts out with lilting and cheery melody that reminds one of the beautiful mountain setting where Brahms wrote his 3rd symphony.   Upon hearing this music, one can almost see the shepherds tending their flocks in an alpine meadow. Suddenly the mood  changes as the music transitions without warning into a vigorous dancelike presto section requiring quick and delicate string playing.

The initial allegretto melody comes back again in the middle of the movement in the form of a march-like minor key variation that interrupts the festivities like a funeral procession invading a lively party.  But the sombre mood does not last long. After another lively section in 3/8 time, the movement ends with a calm restatement of the initial melody.

Updated to MS 3.6


Here's what Wikipedia has to say about Brahm's first symphony:

"Brahms began composing his first symphony in 1854, but much of his work underwent radical changes.  The long gestation of the symphony may be attributed to two factors. First, Brahms' self-critical fastidiousness led him to destroy many of his early works. Second, there was an expectation from Brahms' friends and the public that he would continue "Beethoven's inheritance" and produce a symphony of commensurate dignity and intellectual scope—an expectation that Brahms felt he could not fulfill easily in view of the monumental reputation of Beethoven."

"The value and importance of Brahms' achievements were recognized by Vienna's most powerful critic, the staunchly conservative Eduard Hanslick.  The conductor Hans von Bülow was moved in 1877 to call the symphony "Beethoven's Tenth", due to perceived similarities between the work and various compositions of Beethoven.  It is often remarked that there is a strong resemblance between the main theme of the finale of Brahms' First Symphony and the main theme of the finale of Beethoven's Ninth Symphony. Also, Brahms uses the rhythm of the "fate" motto from the opening of Beethoven's Fifth Symphony. This rather annoyed Brahms; he felt that this amounted to accusations of plagiarism, whereas he saw his use of Beethoven's idiom in this symphony as an act of conscious homage. Brahms himself said, when comment was made on the similarity with Beethoven, "any ass can see that."  Nevertheless, this work is still often referred to as "Beethoven's Tenth".  However, Brahms' horn theme, with the "fate" rhythm, was noted in a letter to Clara Schumann (dated 1868), overheard in an alphorn's playing. "


In this symphony he uses a relatively simple orchestration with A  limited variety of brass and percussion.  There are no tubas or trombones  and only timpani for percussion.  A trio of trombones does make a dramatic appearance in the last movement of this symphony. The brass instruments are used lightly for subtle effects, not too much fortissimo blasting away for the most part.

The winds are lushly scored with doubled parts in a dense, close harmony. Some composers say that his wind orchestration is a bit too thick, but that is a matter of opinion.  The addition of the contrabassoon adds weight to the woodwind section.

The strings are also lushly scored with many double stops and independent melodic lines. The basses often go their own way from the cellos.

I think it sounds *much* better than the original upload, but would be glad to hear what people have to say.

I wasn't satisfied with the acciaccaturas from the B section, so I decided to tweak it for a more natural sound. Also added more rubato.

Enjoy!

Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky's Symphony No. 4 in F minor, Op. 36, was written between 1877 and 1878. Its first performance was at a Russian Musical Society concert in Moscow on February 22, 1878, with Nikolai Rubinstein as conductor. In Middle Europe it sometimes receives the nickname "Fatum", or "Fate".
